title: Could a mysterious object in the Pacific solve the Amelia Earhart mystery?
excerpt: Purdue researchers are investigating a mysterious Pacific object that could provide new clues in the decades-old Amelia Earhart mystery.
content:
For nearly 90 years, the disappearance of Amelia Earhart has remained one of aviation's biggest mysteries. Now, a new expedition hopes a strange object spotted in satellite images could finally provide answers, Purdue University reported.

Earhart vanished on July 2, 1937, while trying to become the first woman to fly around the world. She and navigator Fred Noonan were flying from New Guinea to tiny Howland Island in the Pacific Ocean when radio contact was lost. Neither the pair nor their Lockheed Electra aircraft was ever found, National Geographic said.

This month, researchers from Purdue University and the Archaeological Legacy Institute began a new search centered on Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific nation of Kiribati. The team wants to investigate what is known as the "Taraia Object," a mysterious shape that appears in satellite imagery and older photographs of the island's lagoon.

Some researchers believe the object could be part of Earhart's missing airplane. They plan to use sonar equipment, underwater cameras and other tools to examine the site more closely. If the object is identified as aircraft wreckage, it could become one of the most important discoveries in aviation history, according to Aerotime.

Not everyone agrees. Some longtime Earhart researchers believe the object may be something natural, such as debris or a tree, and say previous searches have not found evidence of the plane there.

Still, the expedition is creating fresh excitement. After decades of dead ends and unanswered questions, researchers hope this latest effort will finally reveal what happened to one of the world's most famous pilots, Yahoo! reported.
